# Kingu: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **Kingu** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**Tiāmat Makes Kingu Her Consort.** After Ea kills Apsû, Tiāmat resolves to avenge the primordial freshwater abyss.  She takes Kingu as her consort and sets him over the gods she has assembled: 'She placed him in the front, leader of the host, to direct the battle, to gain the victory' (Enuma Elish II:122–124, trans.  Foster).

**The Tablet of Destinies.** To legitimate Kingu's command, Tiāmat fastens the Tablet of Destinies (ṭuppi šīmāti) upon his breast.  The tablet is the inscribed record of fates and decrees; to hold it is to hold the power to confirm or cancel the destinies of gods and worlds.  Kingu thus briefly becomes a rival sovereign, and the younger gods are thrown into terror because fate itself seems to have defected to chaos.

**Marduk Defeats Kingu.** Marduk of Babylon accepts single combat with Tiāmat on the condition that the assembly grant him kingship.  After he splits Tiāmat and creates heaven and earth from her body, he turns to her army.  Kingu is captured, stripped of the Tablets, and killed.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Kingu
- **ASCII form:** kingu
- **Meaning:** "Unknown"
- **Domain of influence:** Dragon, Consort of Tiamat
- **Pantheon:** Mesopotamian
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** 𒀭𒆥𒄖
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 224 of 463

## The Name Travels

Kingu is a specifically Babylonian figure, but his narrative pattern — the defeated dragon whose body becomes the stuff of human life — echoes across Near Eastern and later mythologies. The closest parallel is Tiāmat herself: where she becomes the physical cosmos, Kingu becomes the biological substrate of humanity.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Kingu** stands at [/kingu/](/kingu/) — [lore](/kingu/lore/), [scholars](/kingu/scholars/), [patterns](/kingu/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form drops. One is enough to matter, and the label says so plainly: Tier-2.

## The Sources Are Open

The myths above are retold from the temple's record; the primary voices are in the [Sacred Texts](/texts/): [Enūma Eliš](/texts/enuma-elish/) and [The Epic of Gilgamesh](/texts/gilgamesh/). Nothing in this file outranks them.
